1:
A sermon begins here, and the witnesses agree that its first word is an inference. Keil and Delitzsch, reading with grammatical-historical care, note that the Hebrew opens with "and now," by which Moses passes from a contemplation of what the Lord had done for Israel to an exhortation to keep his law: the manifestations of grace laid Israel under obligation to a conscientious observance, that they might continue to enjoy the blessings of the covenant. They map the whole discourse from this hinge — an appeal to hear and keep without adding or taking away, a warning not to forget what happened at Horeb and so fall into image-worship, and a closing threat of dispersion with a promise of restoration. The reformed John Gill fills in what the "therefore" looks back on: God's providing for them and feeding them in the wilderness, preserving them from every hurtful thing, and delivering the two Amorite kings into their hands; for nothing, he says, is a greater incentive to obedience than the kindness and goodness of God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry warns at the outset that this discourse cannot be carved into paragraphs — it is so entire, and its particulars so often repeated, that it must be taken all together and digested into heads. In general it is the use and application of the foregoing history, and Henry turns that into a rule for his readers: this is the use we should make of a review of God's providences toward us, and the histories of ancient times should be improved by us in the same way. The drift of the whole, he adds, is to persuade Israel to keep close to God and not to forsake him for any other, and Moses argues it with a great deal of divine rhetoric, by exhortation and direction and also by motive and argument.

On the demand for attention Henry is exact. Moses does not mean only that they must give him the hearing now, but that whenever the book of the law is read to them or by them they should be attentive to it — hearkening to the statutes as containing the great commands of God and the great concerns of their own souls, and therefore challenging their utmost attention. At Horeb God had made them hear his words, hear them with a witness; and the attention which was then compelled by the circumstances of the delivery ought ever after to be engaged by the excellency of the things themselves. What God spoke once in that way, we should hear twice, and hear often.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the chapter beside Joshua's farewell address, since both press the same point — that Israel should serve Jehovah — and both ground it in his revelation of himself at Horeb as their God. For the two nouns he would say institutions and requirements in modern English; the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley divides them by their objects, the statutes being the laws that concern the worship and service of God and the judgments those that concern duties to men, so that the two together comprehend both tables and the whole law. Ellicott also weighs the order of the promise: life is put before possession, since the penalty of the broken law is death. And the reformed John Calvin states the premise underneath the imperative — the beginning of a good and upright life is to know what is pleasing to God, so Moses first commands them to be teachable and only then admonishes them to prove by their whole life that they have profited in the law.
2:
The rule that guards the law is stated in two directions at once, and the witnesses read the pair as a single fence. Keil and Delitzsch put it as a condition of obedience itself: the observance of the law required that it should be kept as it was given, that nothing should be added and nothing taken away, but that men should submit to it as to the inviolable word of God. Their sharpest point is that the two halves are not unequal in danger — not by omissions only, but by additions also, was the commandment weakened and the word of God turned into ordinances of men, as Pharisaism sufficiently proved. They trace the precept forward: it is repeated later in this book, revived by prophet and proverb, and enforced again at the close of the whole revelation in Revelation 22:18-19; and they take Christ's word that he came not to destroy the law but to fulfil (Matthew 5:17) in the same sense, since the old covenant was not abrogated but glorified and perfected by the new.

Gill allows the words two readings and will not choose between them. On the first, they forbid making new laws of one's own and joining them to the law of God, setting them on a level with it or preferring them before it — as, he says, the Scribes and Pharisees did with their traditions, making the word of God of no effect — and equally forbid abrogating or detracting from what God has given. On the second, the sense is practical rather than textual: neither do what is forbidden nor neglect what is commanded, so that a man is guilty neither of sins of omission nor of commission. Henry reports the same double reading as a disagreement among interpreters — some take it of practice, some of opinion — and gives the second its full weight: you shall not add your own inventions, as if the divine institutions were defective, nor introduce, much less impose, any rites of worship other than what God has appointed; nor shall you set aside anything appointed as needless or superfluous. God's work is perfect, and nothing can be put to it or taken from it without making it worse.

Henry adds a historical observation that turns the verse into a debt we still owe. The Jews understood it as prohibiting any alteration of the text or letter of the law, even in the least jot or tittle; and to their great care and exactness in that, under God, we are very much indebted for the purity and integrity of the Hebrew text. Adam Clarke, reading with wesleyan-arminian plainness, applies the prohibition to the commentator's own trade: add no book, chapter, verse or word which God has not spoken, and give no comment that has any tendency to corrupt, weaken or destroy any part of the revelation.

Ellicott's contribution is a single grammatical point with a long reach. The Hebrew says the word, not the words. The word is the substance of the law; the words in which it is expressed may be more or fewer. On that reading the prohibition does not freeze a wording but protects a thing, and Ellicott draws the consequence out to its furthest edge — that the law of Moses contains in it the germ of all revelation to the very end. Calvin makes the same demand from the side of the hearer: none are to be accounted true disciples of the law but those who obtain their wisdom from it alone, which cannot happen unless men first renounce their own private feelings and then shut their ears against the imaginations of others. He calls the passage a remarkable one, openly condemning whatever man's ingenuity may invent for the service of God.
3:
Moses turns from precept to a piece of very recent memory, and the force of it is that his hearers watched it happen. Gill explains the occasion: Israel had been drawn into the worship of Baal-peor by the daughters of Moab and Midian, through the counsel of Balaam, the fornication leading them into the idolatry, and both highly provoking to God. He notes that the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan render the clause as what the Word of the Lord did to the worshippers of the idol Peor.

Keil and Delitzsch make the pair of verses a demonstration of the principle just laid down, that life is bound up with keeping the law. Israel had just experienced how a faithful observance gives life, in what the Lord had done on account of Baal-peor when he destroyed those who worshipped it, whereas the faithful followers of the Lord remained alive. The Hebrew verb rendered "clave" means to cling to a person and hold fast to him. This example was adduced, they say, precisely because the congregation had passed through it only a very short time before, so that the results of faithfulness on the one hand and of apostasy on the other had been made thoroughly apparent to it. The idiom Moses uses is not "your eyes have seen" but, as Ellicott renders it literally, your eyes are they that see — you are the witnesses of these things.

Ellicott adds a piece of arithmetic that gives the appeal its edge. The men who perished by the plague because of the iniquity at Beth-peor, to the number of twenty-four thousand, seem to have been all members of the younger generation, since Israel had already passed the brook Zered by then. The generation Moses is addressing is therefore not being told about a judgment on their fathers; they are being reminded of one that fell on their own contemporaries.

Calvin builds his whole comment on that fact. The enlargement, he says, shows that the example given in the punishment was so conspicuous that it could not be hidden from even the most ignorant, for Moses is not addressing men of refined judgment here but the common people generally, who had been mere spectators. If God's vengeance had been less manifest, he would not have appealed to them so confidently as witnesses; and their stolidity was so much the less excusable if they were blind to a fact so plain and notorious. Calvin is careful, though, about the praise implied in the second verse. He refers Moses' commendation of their constancy to the present case alone, since it is abundantly clear that they did not persevere in cleaving to God. The meaning, on his reading, is that there was a manifest discrimination in this chastisement, so that the death of the ungodly multitude should preserve the pure worship of God among the survivors.

Gill takes the clinging in the same practical way, as attendance on the service of the sanctuary and observance of the laws — not apostatizing by idolatry or otherwise, but keeping close and following fully. What the two verses set side by side, then, is a plague and a survival within the same camp and the same season, and the survivors are told that they are standing there alive as the evidence.
5:
Moses now points at his own conduct as a specimen of the rule he has just laid down. Gill catches the connection: he had faithfully delivered the statutes and judgments without adding to them or diminishing from them, and had diligently instructed the Israelites in them, taking pains to lead them into a thorough knowledge and understanding of them. Ellicott fastens on the clause about the land, and makes a point that reaches beyond this chapter — it should never be forgotten that there is a special connection between the law of Moses and the land of Canaan, since in many of its precepts it cannot be kept except by a chosen people in a protected land.

What follows turns obedience outward, toward spectators. Keil and Delitzsch state the claim plainly: the laws Moses taught were commandments of the Lord, and keeping and doing them was to be the wisdom and understanding of Israel in the eyes of the nations, who on hearing all these laws would say that this great nation was no other than a wise and understanding people. History, they judge, has confirmed it. Not only did the wisdom of a Solomon astonish the queen of Sheba, but the divine truth Israel possessed in the law attracted the more earnest minds of the heathen world to seek in Israel's knowledge of God the satisfaction of their hearts and the salvation of their souls — especially once, after a short period of bloom, the inward self-dissolution of the heathen religions had set in.

Clarke argues the same case from the state of religion elsewhere. There was no mode of worship at that time on the face of the earth that was not wicked, obscene, puerile, foolish or ridiculous, except the one God had established among the Israelites; and every part of that, taken in its connection, may truly be called a wise and reasonable service. As evidence that the nations did in fact form this opinion, he points to their borrowing: almost all the nations of the earth showed it by taking the principal part of their civil code from this one, and if you take away what Asia and Europe, ancient or modern, have borrowed from the Mosaic laws, you leave little behind that can be called excellent. Wesley makes the same claim more cautiously. Though the generality of the heathen in later ages did, through inveterate prejudice, condemn the laws of the Hebrews, the wisest of them highly approved them, made use of several, and translated them into their own laws and constitutions; and Moses himself has been mentioned with great honour for his wisdom and learning by many of them.

Calvin anticipates the obvious objection and answers it without conceding the point. Someone may reply that the law was unknown to the heathen nations, and that the whole Jewish religion was not merely despised by them but hated. His answer is that other nations are not set up here as judges or arbitrators; the words mean that there will be no nation which, if it should come to a right understanding, would dare to compare itself with Israel, much less prefer itself. Although the doctrine of the law should remain neglected, and even detested, by almost all the world, Moses still declares truly that since God deigned to deliver to this people a rule of life, a stage had been erected before the other nations on which the nobility of that one people would be conspicuous — for it was unreasonable that the glory of God should be tarnished or extinguished by the ignorance of the blind. And Calvin turns the verse into a definition: we are then truly wise when we depend on God's words and submit our feeling to his revelations.
7:
Two questions are asked and neither is answered, because on Moses' account no answer is possible. Gill begins by clearing away the wrong grounds of greatness. Israel was not great for their number, since they were the fewest of all people; nor for the extent of their territory, since the land they were going to possess was a small country; nor for wealth and warlike exploits, though they were not contemptible in either. Their greatness lay in their happy constitution in church and state, being directed and governed in both by laws that came immediately from God himself, and in the knowledge of divine things and the spiritual privileges they were favoured with.

Keil and Delitzsch identify what gave the wisdom of Israel its attracting force. It consisted in this, that in Jehovah they possessed a God who was at hand with his help when they called upon him, as none of the gods of the other nations had ever been; and that in the law of God they possessed such statutes and rights as the heathen never had. From that they draw a general principle worth more than the observation that prompts it: true right has its roots in God, and with the obscuring of the knowledge of God, law and right — with their divinely established foundations — are shaken and obscured as well.

Calvin sets out the two claims as a pair of reasons why the Jews would be celebrated in the whole world. Moses now repeats in his own name what he had put in the mouth of others, as if to show by additional argument that it would actually appear that none were equal to them. The first reason is that God would be ready to afford them help as often as they called upon him; and when Moses says God is nigh to them, Calvin refers it to the presence of his power, abundantly manifested by many miracles. Justly, he adds, does Moses deny that the Gentiles had ever experienced such aid from their gods, since their prayers and cries were offered to deaf and dead idols. The second reason is that God had instructed Israel in perfect righteousness, beyond which nothing could be desired. Wesley opens out the first of the two into its several parts: God was nigh by glorious miracles, by the pledges of his special presence, by the operations of his grace, and particularly by his readiness to hear prayer and to give the succours we call upon him for.

On the second question the witnesses press the word righteous. Gill glosses it as founded in justice and equity, agreeable to right reason, calculated to lead men in the ways of righteousness and truth and to keep them from doing injury to each other's persons and properties, and so to maintain good order, peace and concord. Ellicott finds in the words a claim about the law's position in history — they direct our attention to the law of Moses as distinctly in advance of the age in which it was given. Wesley draws the political moral, and it is the plainest statement of the passage's argument that any of the witnesses makes: Moses implies that the true greatness of a nation does not consist in pomp or power or largeness of empire, as men commonly think, but in the righteousness of its laws.
9:
The exhortation now turns inward, and its first word narrows everything that follows. Keil and Delitzsch render the opening as "only beware and take care of thyself," and explain the phrase about keeping the soul: to keep it is to care for it as the seat of life, to defend one's life from danger and injury. What is not to be forgotten is a set of facts — the things Israel had seen with its own eyes at the mountain — and they are not to depart from the heart as long as life lasts, but to be made known to children and children's children.

The reason those particular facts matter so much is, on their account, the whole difference between one religion and every other. These acts of God formed the foundation of the true religion, the real basis of the covenant legislation, and the firm guarantee of the objective truth and divinity of all the laws and ordinances that Moses gave. That, they say, is what distinguishes the religion of the Old Testament from all heathen religions, whose founders also professed to derive their doctrines and statutes from divine inspiration, but without giving any practical guarantee that their origin was truly divine.

Calvin reads the same opening particle and takes it to mean that this one thing remained. Moses advances by degrees, he says, reminding them that they needed no common heedfulness but must beware with extreme vigilance and diligence, since the slothfulness of the flesh must be spurred on by such instigations, our weakness must be fortified, and we must take measures against our own unsteadfastness — for nothing is easier than that all our zeal should suddenly be forgotten, or gradually grow cold. God had established the certainty of his law as far as was necessary for the grateful and attentive; but not without reason does he ask the people to remember how great is the carelessness of men. And the command reaches past the eyewitnesses: those who saw are to hand down what they saw, that the memory of such remarkable things might be preserved.

Clarke turns each clause into a caution about the soul's estate. Be circumspect and watchful; be mindful of your eternal interests, and whatever becomes of the body, take care of the soul. God does his works that they may be had in everlasting remembrance, and he that forgets them forgets his own mercies. It is not enough to lay up divine things in the memory — they must be laid up in the heart, as David hid God's word in his heart that he might not sin. Clarke presses further than the other witnesses, and says why the exhortation exists at all: those who let the grace of God depart from their hearts lose that grace, and those who lose it fall from it; as some have fallen and risen no more, so may others. Were it impossible for men finally to fall, exhortations of this kind would never have been given, because they would be unnecessary, and God never does an unnecessary thing.

On the command to teach, Clarke makes it a matter of family religion — if a man knows the worth of his own soul he will feel the importance of the souls of his family, and those who neglect family religion neglect personal religion. Ellicott looks instead at how the command fared. It was one which Israel evidently failed to obey, for a generation speedily rose up which knew not Jehovah nor the works he had done (Judges 2:10); and he observes that no trace of a system of national education can be found in Israel until many years later. When education is purely parental, he adds drily, it is likely to be neglected in many instances, since not every parent finds himself able to teach his sons and his sons' sons.
10:
One day is singled out of all the things not to be forgotten. Gill explains why Moses would have this one kept above all others: it was the day the law was given from the mountain, when they saw the fire, the smoke and the lightning, and heard the thunder and the sound of the trumpet, all of which were very shocking and terrifying. He answers the natural objection about the audience, since the men of this generation had been young at the time, under twenty years of age; yet many of them, he says, were old enough to observe these things, and one would think such things should never wear out of their minds. Wesley solves the same difficulty by dividing the hearers: some of them stood there in their own persons, though they were then but young, and the rest in the loins of their parents.

Keil and Delitzsch pick out the leading features of the event as Moses recalls them. First, that God directed him to gather the people together so that he might make known his words to them; and that the purpose of the gathering was twofold — that they might learn to fear him all their life long, and that they might teach their children. The chain of instruction is thus written into the original assembly, not added afterwards as an application.

Ellicott makes that assembly the birthday of a people. The Church of Israel dated from Sinai, he says, as the Church of Christ does from Pentecost; and he notes that the giving of the law appears to have taken place about fifty days after the Passover in Egypt, an association Jewish writers themselves make with the Feast of Pentecost. He finds the same comparison and contrast at work in Paul, where the law given at Sinai is the ministration of death set over against the ministration of the Spirit, the letter that kills against the Spirit that gives life. He also flags a translator's addition — the word "specially" is not in the Hebrew — and insists the day is not merely one special subject of instruction among others but the root of the whole matter. His most striking observation is lexical: the Greek word used for "gather me the people together" is the verb behind the noun for a congregation or church, so that the command might be paraphrased in New Testament language as "form a Church of this people," and the day of the assembly named here and elsewhere as the day of the Church. That, he suggests, is the source of Stephen's phrase about the church in the wilderness (Acts 7:38), and it brings out further the analogy between Israel receiving the letter of the law at Sinai and the gift of the Holy Spirit at Jerusalem.

Calvin uses the verse for a question of authority. Moses explains more fully what he had briefly alluded to before, and he summons the people as eyewitnesses lest they should object that they could not be sure where he had got what he professes was enjoined on him by God. They were all perfectly aware that he had undertaken nothing without God's express command. But Calvin adds a second and better proof, drawn not from testimony but from content: Moses proves from the end and object of the doctrine itself that God was its author, since it tended to nothing else than that God should be purely served and his people be obedient — and nothing can be imagined more just and right than that.
11:
The scene at the mountain is described before its lesson is drawn, and the description is oddly physical. Gill locates the people precisely: they came near and stood under the mountain, that is at the foot of it, in the lower part, as the Targum of Jonathan has it. Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase about the mountain burning with fire unto the midst of heaven as a rhetorical description — burning quite into the sky — of the awful majesty of the pillar of fire in which the glory of the Lord appeared. Ellicott simply cross-references the writer to the Hebrews, who gathered the three nouns of this verse into the blackness and darkness and tempest of Hebrews 12:18.

What the witnesses notice is the combination: fire that reaches to heaven, and at the same time darkness, cloud and thick darkness. The mountain is at once the most visible thing in the wilderness and the least revealing. Israel is brought as close as a people can be brought and is shown nothing but weather and flame.

Calvin makes the verse serve the same argument he has been building since the chapter began, that Moses was only the ambassador and minister of God. The mountain burned in the sight of all the people so that God might be manifested speaking from the midst of the fire — which is to say, the theophany authenticates the speaker rather than displaying the God who speaks. He then takes up the statement that they heard the voice but saw no similitude, and weighs two ways of construing it. It might be read as a kind of concession, the two clauses standing adversatively: although no similitude appeared, yet a voice penetrated even to your ears. But Calvin prefers a stronger reading, that the words were expressly stated in order to show more clearly that this was the voice of God and not one proceeding from a human being — for no man could have concealed himself by any artifice so as to prevent his being seen to speak, whereas they beheld the voice come out of the fire without any external instrumentality.

That last phrase is the pivot of the whole chapter's argument against images, and it is worth noticing how the witnesses reach it. They do not begin from a prohibition and look for reasons; they begin from a remembered scene, and observe what was and was not in it. The people stood at the foot of a burning mountain, in cloud and thick darkness, and heard words. Everything Moses is about to say about graven images rests on that absence, and Keil and Delitzsch state the consequence at once: the Israelites could not see a form of God, but could only hear the voice of his words.
12:
Everything in this chapter's argument against images turns on a negative fact, and here it is stated. Gill sets the scene — the LORD descended on Sinai in a cloud, in fire, and was in the thick darkness, and from there delivered the ten commands. Wesley defines the missing thing: no resemblance of God whereby his essence, properties or actions were represented, such as were usual among the heathen.

Henry works out why a voice and not a shape. God made himself known by a voice of words sounding in their ears, to teach them that faith comes by hearing and that God in the word is nigh us; but no image was presented to the eye, for to see God as he is is reserved for the other world, and to see him as he is not would do us hurt and no good in this one. Probably they expected to see some likeness, since they were ready to break through and gaze; but all they saw was light and fire, and nothing they could make an image of — infinite wisdom so ordering the manifestation because of the peril of idolatry. Henry notes the one exception the record allows, that Moses beheld the similitude of the Lord (Numbers 12:8), and explains it by the man rather than the privilege: God allowed him that favour because he was above the temptation. Hence Henry's own caution: take heed of making images of God in fancy and imagination when we worship him, for there may be idols in the heart where there are none in the sanctuary.

Calvin takes the verse for a confirmation of the second commandment — God manifested himself by a voice and not in a bodily form, whence those not contented with his voice but seeking his visible form substitute imaginations and phantoms in his place. He then raises the objection against himself with unusual candour. God made himself known to the patriarchs in other ways besides a voice: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob knew him not only by hearing but by sight; Moses saw him in the midst of the burning bush; and he manifested himself to the prophets under visible figures, as in the vision of Isaiah 6 and those of Ezekiel. The argument from a voice heard without a form does not, on the face of it, look valid, since visible forms have often been exhibited in which he testified his presence.

His solution is twofold. First, that although God may have invested himself in certain forms in order to manifest himself, this must be accounted a peculiar circumstance and not a general rule. Second, that the visions shown to the patriarchs were testimonies of his invisible glory, given to elevate men's minds to things above rather than to keep them entangled among earthly elements. In promulgating his law, Calvin adds, God first prescribed what believers must follow, as the best method of retaining their minds in true religion and the best remedy for idolatry: when he gathered a Church to himself and handed down an inviolable rule for holy living, he had not invested himself in a bodily shape but had exhibited the living image of his glory in the doctrine itself. Whoever seeks God in a visible figure therefore does not merely decline but actually revolts from the true study of piety. And if it is objected that God is not inconsistent with himself, the reply is easy: whenever he appeared to the patriarchs in a visible form he gave a temporary sign, which is no contradiction of this commandment. Isaiah saw the Lord of hosts on his throne, and yet cries out as from the mouth of God, to whom will ye liken me (Isaiah 40:25) — on the same principle as Moses, that the nature of God is corrupted if a corruptible thing be called his image.
13:
The content of what the voice said is now named, and the name it is given is covenant. Gill explains why the law should be called that: because it contained, on God's part, things he would have done or avoided, to which were annexed promises of long life and happiness in the land he was giving them; and because on their part they agreed to hearken to it and obey it. A covenant, on that account, is not merely a set of requirements but a set of requirements with terms attached and consent given.

Keil and Delitzsch keep the sequence exact. The Israelites could not see a form of God; they could only hear the voice of his words, when the Lord proclaimed his covenant to them and uttered the ten words — which he afterwards gave to Moses written upon two tables of stone. The order matters to the chapter's argument. What Israel received at Horeb was first a voice, then a text; the permanent form the revelation took was writing, not a likeness, and the stone carried words rather than any image of the God who spoke them.
14:
A distinction is being drawn between two bodies of instruction, and the witnesses agree on where the line falls. Keil and Delitzsch put it in sequence: when the Lord himself had made known to the people in the ten words the covenant which he commanded them to do, he then directed Moses to teach them the laws and rights they were to observe in Canaan — that is, the statutes of the Sinaitic legislation which follow from Exodus 21 onwards. The ten words came directly from God to the whole nation; the rest came through a teacher. Gill fixes the moment at which the second commission was given: when the ten commandments had been delivered on the mount and Moses was ordered to come up to God there. Wesley labels the two classes plainly — the statutes and judgments here are the ceremonial and judicial laws, which are in this way distinguished from the moral law, or the ten commandments.

Henry, taking the whole discourse together, shows how that threefold division was meant to work in practice. God's commandments were the way Israel must keep in and the rule they must keep to: they must govern themselves by the moral precepts, perform their devotion according to the divine ritual, and administer justice according to the judicial law. Each part of the law had a department of life assigned to it, and none of the three was optional.

Henry also tracks the charge itself through the chapter, and this verse is one of its stations. Moses charges them to keep God's commandments, to do them here and earlier in the address, to keep and do them together, and to perform the covenant — the same demand repeated under different verbs until it cannot be mistaken for advice. Hearing must be in order to doing, and knowledge in order to practice.

The clause about the land does real work in the argument. What Moses taught was not given to be admired in the wilderness but to be done across the Jordan, and Keil and Delitzsch name Canaan as the place of its observance twice in a single sentence. That is why the commission to teach is dated to Horeb but aimed at the country on the other side of the river.
15:
The negative fact of the last few verses is now turned into a command, and Keil and Delitzsch state the inference in one line: as the Israelites had seen no shape of God at Horeb, they were to beware for their souls' sake of acting corruptly and making any kind of image of Jehovah their God — and, as the context shows, the thing forbidden is making one in order to worship God in it. The phrases that follow, they add, are in apposition to the graven image and serve to explain and emphasize the prohibition rather than to extend it.

Clarke draws the principle out from the divine side. However God chose to appear or manifest himself, he took care never to assume any describable form; he would have no image-worship, because he is a Spirit, and they who worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth. His objection to images is psychological as much as theological: these outward things tend to draw the mind out of itself and diffuse it upon sensible, if not sensual, objects, so that spiritual worship is prevented and the Holy Spirit grieved; persons acting in this way, he says bluntly, can never know much of the religion of the heart. Wesley makes the same point from the singularity of the occasion — God, who in other places and times did appear in a similitude in the fashion of a man, purposely avoided all such representation at this most solemn appearance, when he came to give eternal laws, in order to show that he abhors the worship of images, or of himself by images of whatever kind, because he is the invisible God.

Ellicott is the one witness who registers how hard the demand was. The difficulty of learning to worship one whom we cannot see is, happily, one which our education does not enable us to realise as Israel had to; all the nations round about had their visible symbols of deity, and centuries later the world would describe the followers of Christ as atheists precisely because they had no visible God. It is recorded in special praise of Moses, he notes, that he endured as seeing him who is invisible.

On the word corrupt the witnesses converge from different directions. Gill observes that idolatry corrupts not only the worshippers but the word and worship of God. Henry reads the verb as debauch, and explains the mechanism: those who think to make images of God form in their minds such notions of him as must be an inlet to all impieties, and it is intimated that this is a spiritual adultery — to represent an infinite Spirit by an image, and the great Creator by the image of a creature, is the greatest affront we can put upon God and the greatest cheat we can put upon ourselves. Ellicott finds the connection between idolatry and corruption to be twofold: first it changes the glory of the incorruptible God into an image of his corruptible creatures; and secondly it always ends by corrupting the idolater, since man was made to have dominion over the works of God's hands and cannot worship anything in creation which he was not intended to rule. He can only fulfil his destiny by striving after the divine likeness, rising to what is above him instead of stooping to what is below. Clarke, for his part, names the deities the clause about male and female has in view — Baal-peor and the Roman Priapus, Ashtaroth or Astarte, and the Venus of the Greeks and Romans — after whom, he says, most nations of the world literally went a whoring.
17:
The catalogue descends through the ranks of creation — beast, bird, creeping thing, fish — and the witnesses read it as a survey of what the surrounding world actually worshipped. Gill's remark is the driest: there is scarcely a creature in the list whose likeness has not been made and worshipped, or the creature itself adored, and he instances the ox among the Egyptians, the sheep among the Thebans, and the goat among the Mendesians.

Clarke fills out the Egyptian half of the picture at close range. He names the god Apis, worshipped under the form of a white bull; the ibis and the hawk among the birds, which had divine honours paid to them; serpents and the crocodile among the reptiles; and then, running past the point where the list can be taken seriously, monkeys, dogs, cats, the scarab beetle, leeks and onions. Keil and Delitzsch make the same historical connection with more restraint, taking the prohibition of animal images as a caution against imitating the animal worship of Egypt; and Ellicott says only that there may be an allusion to the animal idolatry of Egypt here.

Gill treats the creeping things separately and traces them to a single origin. Serpents were worshipped by many, and indeed that creature is introduced into almost all the idolatries of the heathen — which seems to him to take its rise from the serpent Satan made use of to deceive our first parents. Whatever weight one gives that derivation, it registers something the catalogue itself implies: the list is not random, and each of its classes had real altars behind it.

Henry gathers the whole sequence into a single instruction and a single argument. Whatever you do, he has Moses say, make no similitude of God — not in a human shape, male or female, nor in the shape of any beast or fowl, serpent or fish; for the heathen worshipped their gods by images of all these kinds, being either not able to form, or not willing to admit, the plain demonstration the prophet makes when he says that the workman made it, therefore it is not God. That is the argument the catalogue is built to produce. Reading down the ranks of creation, from the figure of a man to the fish in the water, the hearer is asked at every step to notice that he is being offered something God made as a likeness of the God who made it.
19:
The last and most respectable form of idolatry is taken up separately, and the witnesses concede that it is the hardest to argue against. Gill grants that lifting up the eyes to the starry heaven is not in itself sinful, and may be commendably done, to raise admiration at the works of God and lead a man to adore their author; but if not guarded against it may be ensnaring. Clarke calls the worship of the heavenly bodies the oldest species of idolatry, and explains its plausibility: those without knowledge of the true God took the sun, moon and stars for self-existing authors of every blessing mankind possesses. He credits its decline to a science — a rational system of astronomy destroyed the superstition, and little of it now remains except among a few astrologers, whom he treats severely. Ellicott adds that even the purest worship of antiquity, that of the Persians, hardly escaped this snare.

Henry notices the verb Moses chooses. The caution is against being driven to worship them, by the strong impulse of a vain imagination and the impetuous torrent of the customs of the nations; the heart is supposed to walk after the eye, which in our degenerate state it is apt to do. Seeing the sun and the stars, a man will so admire their height and brightness, their regular motion and powerful influence, that he will be tempted to give them the glory due to him who made them what they are to us. Yet Henry thinks the temptation weak to anyone who will use his reason, and his reason is the one Moses gives: these pretended deities are man's servants, ordained to give light on earth — and shall we serve what was made to serve us? He points to the Hebrew name of the sun, which signifies a servant, since it holds the candle to all mankind.

Calvin adds a second layer to the temptation. Moses not only recalls them from the error of thinking these are so many gods, but anticipates a subtler superstition — that, ravished by the brightness of the stars, men should conceive them to be somehow of God. Since God represents his glory in the heavenly host, Satan under that very pretext stupefies men's minds, so that they attempt to worship God in these luminaries and stumble at the very threshold. Hence Moses declares that they must not even lean on heavenly creatures, since God's majesty is superior to sun and moon and all the stars. The word divided, Calvin says, implies subjection, as if the sun were our minister and the moon with all the stars our handmaid; yet it also commends God's providence in their varied course, for the sun does not warm all lands at one moment, the moon has her circuits, and the stars rise and set as the heaven revolves. What aggravates the sin is that Israel would be serving what ministers to the heathen too: what can be more unworthy, he asks, than for the children of God to worship the sun, the servant of all the world? Wesley says the same in a sentence — these are not gods but creatures, made not for the worship but for the use of men.

On the last clause the grammatical witnesses break from an old consensus. Keil and Delitzsch say the thought is not that God gave the heathen sun, moon and stars for service, to serve them with their light — the view of Onkelos, the Rabbins and Jerome — but that he allotted them to the nations for worship, permitting them to choose them as the objects of their religion. Ellicott reaches the same end another way: the heavenly bodies were never the special protectors of any one nation, whereas Jehovah was pledged to be the God of Israel — the argument, he judges, of the two verses together.
20:
Against the borrowed gods of the last verse Moses sets a piece of Israel's own history, and the image he uses for it is a furnace. Gill explains the figure from metallurgy: the allusion is to the trying and melting of metals and the freeing of them from dross by putting them into furnaces strongly heated, some made of earth and others of iron, the word here signifying the kind in which gold and silver are melted. Egypt is compared to an iron furnace because of the cruelty with which the Israelites were used in it, the hardships they were put under and the bondage they were kept in — and out of all of it the Lord brought them, as he does all his people out of their afflictions, sometimes called the furnace of affliction, where their graces are tried and they are purged and refined from their dross.

Clarke reads the same words far more literally, and gets a different picture of Egyptian labour out of them. From this mention of an iron furnace, he says, there can be little doubt that the Israelites were employed in Egypt in the most laborious works of metallurgy; and he adds the detail that makes the sentence land — digging, smelting and forging iron in so hot a climate must have been oppressive work indeed. Whether the phrase is a figure for suffering or a memory of a trade is not settled by the verse, and the witnesses simply take it different ways.

Keil and Delitzsch use the verse to complete the argument of the whole section. The Israelites were not to imitate the heathen in the matter of star-worship, because Jehovah, who brought them out of the iron furnace of Egypt, had taken them to himself — that is, had drawn them out and separated them from the rest of the nations to be a people of inheritance. The verb is the point: what the other nations received was an allotment of the heavenly bodies; what Israel received was a taking, a separation to God's own possession. From that they draw the practical consequence for worship: Israel was therefore not to seek God or pray to him in any kind of creature, but to worship him without image and form, in a manner corresponding to his own nature, which had been manifested in no form and therefore could not be imitated.

The two halves of the verse thus answer each other. Egypt is where they were melted; Israel is what they were made. And the phrase Keil and Delitzsch gloss as a people of inheritance is the same idea as the peculiar treasure of the earlier covenant — a nation held not as one among the many under the divided heavens, but as property. Gill's reading and theirs converge here, whatever the furnace originally described: a people brought out of a fire has no business bowing to the lights that shine on everybody.
21:
The mention of the land carries Moses to his own exclusion from it, and the witnesses treat the interruption as deliberate. Keil and Delitzsch trace the sequence: the bringing of Israel out of Egypt reminds Moses of the end, which is Canaan, and that leads him to mention again how the Lord had refused him permission to enter this good land — after which he returns to the warning not to forget the covenant or make any image, since Jehovah as a jealous God would never tolerate it. Gill notes only where the sentence ends for Moses himself: he died in a mountain of Moab, and in a valley there he was buried.

A textual difficulty sits in the middle of the passage, and Keil and Delitzsch meet it head on. Moses says God swore that he should not cross the Jordan; but no such oath is mentioned in the account of the offence at the waters of strife, nor at the announcement of Moses' death in Numbers 27:12. Knobel took the silence as evidence against the statement. Their answer is that it is not to be called in question on that ground, since it is perfectly obvious from the earlier chapter of this book, where Moses recalls his pleading with God, that all the details are not given in the historical account of the event.

Clarke turns the fact into an argument aimed straight at the hearers, and it is the shortest and sharpest thing said on the passage: the Lord was angry with me — and if with me, so as to debar me from entering the promised land, can you think to escape if you are guilty of greater provocations?

Calvin is anxious that the reason for the mention be understood correctly. Moses records that it arose from the transgression of the people that he was not permitted to enter, not by way of expostulation, and much less to accuse God of cruelty, as though he had been improperly and unjustly substituted as a criminal in the place of others, but rather to magnify the goodness of God toward those whom he had treated with so much indulgence. The comparison is the thing to notice: they were to enjoy the land, and he was to be kept out of it. He must die in this land of Moab, while to them it is given to enjoy the promised inheritance. So they are upbraided with their guilt in such a way that all the bitterness of the reproof is sweetened by the sense of God's mercy — that by that sweetness they might be ravished into admiration, when they understand how mercifully the pardon is extended to them which was denied to Moses.

Two smaller points close the passage. Calvin notes that the phrase rendered "for your sakes" might as well be "for your words," or even "for your affairs," since the Hebrew noun covers a man's business as well as his speech; and although Moses had been driven to his sin by their rebellious clamours, he states simply that he was punished on their account. And to the objection that he lays the blame on men who were mostly dead by now, Calvin answers that many of them were still surviving, and that it is no novelty for the children to be included with the fathers when the whole body of a people has sinned.
23:
The warning is repeated for the third time in the chapter, and Gill gives the reason for the repetition in a line: Moses would not be long with them to advise, instruct and caution them. Henry takes up the object of the warning, which is not idolatry directly but forgetting. Though God is ever mindful of the covenant, we are apt to forget it, and this is at the bottom of all our departures from God; we have need therefore to watch against everything that would put the covenant out of our minds, and to watch over our own hearts lest at any time we let it slip. Care and caution and holy watchfulness, he says, are the best helps against a bad memory.

Calvin begins by clearing away an apparent inconsistency in the way the prohibition is stated. Moses first forbids that idols should be made at all, and afterwards speaks only of worshipping and adoring them — but there is no contradiction in the sense, since it is already in itself a wicked error to attribute any image to God, and another superstition always accompanies it, namely that God is improperly worshipped in this visible symbol. The two prohibitions are one because the two acts are inseparable in practice.

From there he restates the principle he has been building through the chapter, and it is stated more strongly here than anywhere else. Whatever holds down and confines our senses to the earth is contrary to the covenant of God; for in that covenant, inviting us to himself, he permits us to think of nothing but what is spiritual, and therefore sets his voice against all the imaginations by which heathen nations have always been deceived — deceived because they were deprived of the light of that doctrine which would direct them to the heavenly greatness of God himself. Those who have been taught by God's law not only that he alone is to be worshipped but that he may not be represented by any visible effigy are justly accounted covenant-breakers if they do not confine themselves within those bounds, since they violate the very commandment by which they are told to worship God spiritually.

Calvin also notices a small grammatical question in the closing clause, and settles it as a comparison rather than a relative: the sense is that they must do as the Lord their God has commanded them. On that reading the meaning of Moses is by no means obscure, and Calvin states it as a rule of obedience with no room left in it — we must simply obey God's word, and must not dispute whether what he has forbidden is lawful or not, nor seek any other rule of right than following what he has prescribed. He applies it at once to the argument of his own century. Let his opponents dispute as they please that images are not to be removed because they are useful for the people's instruction; but let this be our wisdom, to acquiesce in what God has chosen to decree in the matter. The verse, on his reading, is not primarily about art or its uses. It is about whether a command needs to be found reasonable before it is kept.
24:
The warning ends in two names for God, and the witnesses take them as the ground of everything said before. Gill applies the first to God's enemies: his wrath is like fire to burn up and destroy all who oppose him and break his commands, and idolaters especially, whose sin of all others is the most provoking, since it strikes at his being, his honour and his glory. Wesley expands both names together — a just and terrible God, who notwithstanding his special relation to Israel will severely punish them if they provoke him; and a jealous God, who being espoused to them will be highly incensed if they follow after other lovers, and will bear no rival or partner.

Clarke sets the phrase against two things his hearers had actually seen, and the contrast is the sharpest thing said on the verse. They had seen God on the mount as an unconsuming fire, while he appeared to Moses and gave the law; and they had seen him as a consuming fire in the case of Korah, Dathan and Abiram and their company. The same element had shown itself to them in both characters within the same generation, so that they had every good to expect from his approbation and every evil to dread from his displeasure.

Henry divides the two names by what each implies about God's dealing with an affront. As a jealous God he has an eye to discern one: he must have the entire affection and adoration of his people, and will by no means endure a rival — and God's jealousy over us, Henry adds, is a good reason for our godly jealousy over ourselves. As a consuming fire he has a heavy hand to punish it, and especially in his worship, for there he is jealous in a special manner. Yet Henry refuses to leave the argument on that side alone. Considering what a God he is with whom we have to do, we should make conscience of our duty and not dare to sin against him; but the question he actually presses is the other one — shall we forsake a merciful God, who will never forsake us if we are faithful to him? Whither can we go? Let us be held to our duty by the bonds of love, and prevailed with by the mercies of God to cleave to him.

Ellicott follows the phrase into the New Testament, where it is quoted at the end of a chapter that has just contrasted Sinai with something greater. The writer to the Hebrews takes up these words, he observes, to enforce the lessons not of Sinai but of Pentecost, and of the voice of him who speaks from heaven by the Spirit he has sent. The description is not left behind with the older covenant; it is transferred to the newer one, and applied to hearers who have come not to a mountain that burned with fire but to a voice from heaven.
25:
The warning now takes the long view, and its danger is not persecution but settlement. Gill reads the opening clause as a measure of time — children and grandchildren, several ages and generations passed. Keil and Delitzsch set out the supposed case in full: if the Israelites should beget children and children's children, and grow old in the land, and then make images of God and do what displeased him to provoke him. They are careful about what growing old in the land is meant to imply. It involves forgetfulness of the former manifestations of grace on the Lord's part; it does not necessarily mean becoming voluptuous through the enjoyment of the riches of the country, although that too might lead to forgetting God and his mercies.

Ellicott finds the whole peril compressed into one Hebrew verb. The phrase rendered "shall have remained long" is literally shall slumber, which he calls a very suggestive expression, and he draws the modern application without softening it: prosperity often sends true religion to sleep, and brings conventional, or fashionable, religion in its stead. On that reading the apostasy Moses fears does not arrive as a decision. It arrives as a drowsiness, in a generation that has never known anything to be afraid of.

Calvin explains why the warning is put in terms of descendants at all. Moses had already forbidden them to turn aside to idols; he now requires that this instruction be handed down to their grandchildren and their whole race, as if to say that they must continue faithfully in the pure worship of God — not only lest they be kept out of the land, but lest, after long and quiet possession of it, they should be expelled from it. Long possession, Calvin observes, might have hardened their minds in security and arrogance, as if they had no change to fear. So that as time passed they should not trust that they were firmly established and advance to greater licence, Moses reminds them that the punishment already threatened would reach their descendants too; for it was no less easy for God to drive their distant posterity out of a quiet nest than it would have been to prevent their taking possession of it in the first place.

Calvin also notes the widening of the subject as the passage goes on. Although Moses adverts at the outset only to idolatry, he takes occasion from it to inveigh generally against transgressors of the law and to denounce punishment on them, so that what begins as a caution about images ends as a statement of the curse that overhangs all despisers of God. That is why the sentence is built as a supposition stretching over generations rather than as a rule: what is being described is not an act but a drift, and the remedy Moses prescribes for it is the one he prescribed at the start of the sermon, that the thing be handed down to children and children's children.
26:
Moses now swears, and the witnesses take some interest in what exactly he is summoning. Gill treats the appeal as a matter of publicity: the caution had been given so strongly and so openly that heaven and earth could be called to testify that the law forbidding idolatry had been set before them. Clarke recognises the form at once as a most solemn method of adjuration, in use among all the nations of the world, and quotes the parallel from Virgil, where Aeneas draws his sword and calls the Sun to witness, and the earth, and the springs and rivers, and whatever powers lie beneath the deep or tread the golden sky, to hear and attest his vow. God and man being called upon to bear testimony, Clarke explains, the purpose is that if there were any flaw or insincerity it might be detected, and if any crime, it might not go unpunished — and such appeals, he adds, show at once both the origin and the use of oaths.

What the two witnesses actually are is disputed. One old exposition takes heaven and earth as a figure of speech for the intelligent creatures in them, and especially for angels and men, on the ground that none but a rational creature can properly bear witness. Calvin dismisses that reading as a poor one, and prefers to let the personification stand: Moses calls on heaven and earth as if even things inanimate and without reason were in a manner conscious of the vengeance of God. He notes the same figure elsewhere in Moses' own song and in Isaiah's opening indictment, where the prophet addresses his words to the heavens and the earth in order to shame a stupefied people; and he explains the point of it — to call heaven and earth to witness God's vengeance is as much as to say that it will appear as clearly as heaven and earth appear before our eyes.

Keil and Delitzsch take the same side and state it with more precision. Heaven and earth do not stand here for the rational beings dwelling in them; they are personified, represented as living and capable of sensation and speech, and cited as witnesses who would rise up against Israel. But the office they are given is exact: they are not summoned to proclaim Israel's guilt, but to bear witness that God, the Lord of heaven and earth, had warned the people. The witnesses testify to the warning, not to the crime — which is why they can be called now, before anything has happened, and why the summons functions as a last mercy rather than a verdict.

Calvin adds one more reason for the form Moses chooses. The threat is put this way in order that it may affect them more deeply; a warning delivered before the whole visible creation is harder to forget than one delivered in private. The two things Moses can point at are the sky over the camp and the ground under it, and he makes both of them parties to the transaction.
27:
The sentence is now pronounced, and it has two parts: a scattering, and what the scattered people will find themselves doing. Gill identifies the first with the two captivities — the ten tribes dispersed among the cities of the Medes, the two tribes throughout the empire of Babylon — and Clarke says it was amply verified in their captivities and dispersions. Keil and Delitzsch refuse to fix it to one event. Against Knobel, who thought the author had the Assyrian period in view, they hold that the threat covers all the dispersions coming on the rebellious nation in future times, down to the dispersion under the Romans which continues still. Ellicott warns that our familiarity with the fact as history must not blind us to its force as prophecy, and finds in it an argument about purpose: that the Jews were taken captive for idolatry and dispersed afterwards is to him a remarkable proof that the reason they were brought into Canaan and kept there was to be witnesses for Jehovah.

The second half of the threat is harder, and here the witnesses genuinely divide. Gill takes it at face value first: they would be enticed into the service of idols made by men and cut out of wood and stone, which is a more brutish and stupid thing than worshipping the sun and moon and stars, since those at least are not the works of men's hands but the glorious works of the eternal God. But he immediately records the objection, which is historical — in their captivities the Israelites were not in fact given to idolatry but were cured of it there. That difficulty produces a second reading, which Gill reports from the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan: the phrase means serving the people who serve idols, not the idols themselves. Ellicott takes that line and finds support for it in Rashi — you shall be in bondage to them, being ruled by their worshippers. He explains how the two senses come to be interchangeable, since the cause of a people and the cause of its idols are so constantly identified in the Old Testament that those in bondage to a nation may be described as in bondage to its gods; the gods were even held to share the captivity, as Isaiah says of Bel and Nebo that they could not deliver but are themselves gone into captivity. Gill thinks what follows in the verse confirms the first and plainer sense.

Keil and Delitzsch read the threat as a law of decline rather than a prediction of one episode. There among the heathen they would serve gods that were the work of men's hands, of wood and stone, which could neither hear nor eat nor smell — that is, possessed no senses and showed no sign of life. What Moses threatens follows, they say, from the eternal laws of the divine government: the more refined idolatry of image-worship leads to coarser and coarser forms, in which the whole nature of idol-worship is manifested in all its pitiableness. They quote Schultz to the same effect — when once the God of revelation is forsaken, the God of reason and imagination must soon be given up as well, making way for still lower powers.

Wesley draws the moral that ties the two halves together: the very thing which was their choice shall be their punishment, it being just and usual with God to punish one sin by giving men up to another. Clarke ends elsewhere, on the ten tribes whose place of residence no man now knows with certainty; that they still exist he does not doubt, though they are probably so incorporated with the idolaters among whom they dwell as to be no longer distinguishable — yet God, he adds, can gather them.
29:
The threat turns, on one word, into a promise, and the witnesses all notice where the seeking is done from. Gill spells out both the place and the manner: even out of those depths of affliction and distress, scattered about in the world and in the uttermost parts of it, they may seek God by prayer and supplication, acknowledging and confessing sin, and desiring that he would be gracious and forgive and bring them out of their miserable condition. Wesley states the principle behind it in two sentences that carry further than their length: whatever place we are in, we may from thence seek him — there is no part of the earth which has a gulf fixed between it and heaven.

Keil and Delitzsch find the same movement in a parable. From thence Israel would come to itself again in the time of deepest misery, like the prodigal son in the gospel, would seek the Lord its God, and would find him — if it sought with all its heart and with all its soul. The condition is not an afterthought; it is the substance of what the promise offers. Clarke reads it as an open door and turns it into a question about his own century: God is longsuffering and of tender mercy, and waits, ever ready, to receive a backsliding soul when it returns to him — and is not this promise left on record for the encouragement and salvation of lost Israel?

Calvin gives the pastoral reason for the promise standing where it does, immediately after the threat. Moses exhorts and encourages them in the confidence of obtaining pardon, and by doing so anticipates them, so that they might not be overwhelmed with sorrow when smitten by God's hand; for despair, he says, awakens such rage in the wretched that they cannot submit themselves to God. He therefore sets before them another object in their punishments, that they may not cease to taste God's goodness in the midst of their afflictions, by which he is inviting them to repentance — since the sinner will never set about seeking God unless he thinks him accessible to prayer.

But Calvin will not let the promise be claimed cheaply, and he reads the doubled phrase about heart and soul as the guard against that. Moses warns them to return truly and sincerely to a sound mind, because they will gain nothing by false profession; nothing is more common than to complain to God whenever we are oppressed with troubles and then, when they are at all intermitted, to return immediately to our natural state. Sincere conversion is therefore what is prescribed, for "all the heart" is precisely equivalent to an upright heart, contrasted with a double or feigned one. And then he adds the qualification that keeps the demand from crushing the person it is addressed to. This must be noted, he says, lest a sense of our infirmity should disturb us; since it is not possible for men to give themselves wholly to God, the knowledge of their own inability is apt to induce listlessness — whereas, provided we do not deal deceitfully, our penitence is declared to be approved by God.
30:
The promise is now dated and grounded. Gill locates the tribulation concretely — in a strange land, in the power of a foreign enemy, and used ill — and Wesley glosses the latter days simply as succeeding ages. Keil and Delitzsch treat the two verses as the close of the whole picture of the future: all these things will befall Israel in its trouble, and at the end of the days it will turn to Jehovah its God and hearken to his voice. They note that returning and hearkening both presuppose something, namely that the Lord will be found by those who earnestly seek him; and the ground of that assurance is given in the next verse, that he is a merciful God who does not let his people go, nor destroy them, nor forget the covenant with the fathers. The Hebrew verb behind "forsake," they observe, means to let loose or to withdraw the hand from a person.

Calvin uses the pair of verses to say what afflictions are for. He appeals to the apostle's saying that no chastening for the present seems joyous but grievous, yet afterward yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness to those exercised by it (Hebrews 12:11), and says experience confirms it. So that Israel should not be provoked to wrath by God's stripes, Moses reminds them of the usefulness of those stripes — because they would never turn to God unless aided by this remedy. Then Calvin sets out the two grounds of hope the passage supplies, and ranks them. God will be willing to be appeased because he is by nature merciful; but Moses adds a second confirmation, more certain and more familiar than an appeal to the divine nature, namely that God had adopted this people by a perpetual covenant. Character is the deeper reason; a covenant is the one a frightened people can hold on to.

Gill reads the title in the same direction and pushes it further back: God is a merciful God in Christ, in whom he has proclaimed his name as such — a view of which Moses had a comfortable sight, so that he could attest it from his own knowledge and experience. The claim being made is thus not that God will overlook the apostasy, but that the covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob is older than the apostasy and will outlast it.

Clarke turns the promise on the present and finds it unfulfilled. Are not these the times spoken of, he asks, and is there still hope for Israel? Could we see them become zealous for their own law and observances, humble themselves before the God of Jacob, conduct their public worship with any tolerable decency, and inquire the road to Zion with their faces thitherward, then we might hope that the redemption of Israel was at hand. But he sees no distant evidence of anything of the kind, except in a very few solitary instances, and ends with the prophet's question rather than an answer: by whom shall Jacob arise, for in this sense he is small?
32:
The last movement of the sermon is an argument from evidence, and it opens by inviting an investigation. Gill reads the summons as a call to research — inquire into and consult the annals of former times, of ages past. Calvin, who reaches nearly the same conclusion by a different route, explicitly rejects that construction of the phrase: he will not take "the days that are past" to mean annals or chronicles, and equally dismisses the more refined exposition by which all creatures above and below are made witnesses. He makes no question that Moses simply desires them to inquire and examine whether, from the creation of the world or in any most remote region, any such thing had ever come to pass. Wesley reads the second half of the sweep in the same practical way: from one side of heaven to the other means of the earth under heaven, and the command is to ask all the inhabitants of the world.

Calvin explains what the comparison is for. Moses here more forcibly extols and pronounces magnificent praises on the miracles he had before related more simply, his object being to produce a fuller conviction of the dignity of the law. He magnifies them by comparison, because nothing like them had ever occurred; and the reasoning is exact — if any such instance had previously taken place, some portion of the event's preciousness or honour would have been taken away from it. Since from the beginning of the world only one such illustrious manifestation of God's power had been given, it afforded the law the greater sanction. And Moses adds that if they were to search over the whole world they would nowhere find anything similar.

Keil and Delitzsch explain why the argument comes here rather than earlier, and what it is meant to accomplish that the threats could not. Moses is aiming at something more than merely preventing apostasy by the fear of punishment: he wants to secure a more faithful attachment and a continued obedience by awakening the feeling of cordial love. So he reminds them once more of the glorious miracles of divine grace performed in connection with the election and deliverance of Israel, such as had never been heard of from the beginning of the world; and with this strong practical proof of the love of the true God he brings his first address to a close.

Ellicott finds the same argument used afterwards by Paul, and used for a purpose Moses does not state here. The reasoning that the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29) is, on his reading, this verse turned toward the future: God did not go and take himself a nation out of the midst of another nation in order to abandon them at the last. He never did so much in the way of personal and visible interposition for any people, and he will not forsake the work of his own hands. Ellicott adds that Moses had himself proved the truth of this in many a scene of sin and peril averted by his own intercession — which gives the question in the verse a weight beyond rhetoric, since the man asking it had tested the answer.
33:
The first of the two unparalleled things is a voice heard and survived, and the emphasis falls on the surviving. Gill piles up the degrees: none ever heard the voice of God as they did, much less speaking such words as they heard, and still less out of the midst of fire. Wesley glosses the last clause with the fear it answers — they lived, and were not overwhelmed and consumed by such a glorious appearance.

Clarke explains why that should have been in doubt at all. It seems to have been a general belief, he says, that if God appeared to men it was for the purpose of destroying them; and indeed most of the extraordinary manifestations of God were in the way of judgment. Here it was different. He sets out what happened in three steps, and the third is the point of the verse. They heard his voice speaking with them in a distinct, articulate manner; they saw the fire, the symbol of his presence, whose appearances demonstrated it to be supernatural; and notwithstanding that God appeared so terrible, no person was destroyed — for he came not to destroy, but to save.

Calvin takes the verse as the place where the transcendency of the whole event is stated most openly, and defends it against the obvious objection. It is true, he grants, that the superstitions of the Gentiles had been confirmed of old by many apparitions; but among all the portents which wretched men have imagined for their own willing self-deception there is nothing that approaches this miracle. His reason is not that the story is more impressive but that it is differently attested. Many have individually lied, and their false and foolish tales have been rashly believed; but here we have not to do with unfounded and scattered rumours, nor with the dreams of some single person. Moses produces more than seven hundred thousand witnesses, to whom the glory of God had clearly and certainly appeared.

That argument is worth pausing on, because it is the hinge of the appeal Moses has been making since the chapter began. Everything in the sermon rests on a claim about eyewitnesses — your eyes have seen, the day thou stoodest before the LORD, ye came near and stood under the mountain — and Calvin here states the logic underneath it. A private vision can be doubted because only one man can check it. A national one is exposed to the memory of everybody who was there, which is precisely why Moses can appeal to his hearers as evidence rather than asking them to take his word. Calvin adds that God had never assayed to do the same again, but had afforded this solitary instance in order to render his law illustrious in all ages.
34:
The second unparalleled thing is a nation extracted whole from the middle of another, and Gill states the claim precisely: God had not only assayed to do this but had actually done it, and no instance like it could be produced — especially none done in the manner this was. Calvin presses the same point on the material Moses names. God took him a nation from the midst of a nation: by his incomparable power he rescued the descendants of Abraham, who, though dispersed through Egypt and as it were enclosed in its bowels, were an obscure and ignoble part of a most famous people. And he notes that the verse is not confined to the giving of the law but reaches over the whole course of the deliverance, since it names temptations and signs in general.

Clarke sets out what made the exodus so improbable, and the list is a piece of plain reasoning rather than rhetoric. A whole people, upwards of six hundred thousand effective men besides women and children, was brought out of the midst of a very powerful nation to whose economy their services were essential, and brought out without striking a blow; the departure was open and public; the sea itself was supernaturally divided to give the host a passage; and in a desert utterly unfriendly to human life they were sustained for forty years.

He then works through the seven means the verse names, and the sequence turns out to be graded. Temptations he derives from a root meaning to try or prove — the miracles wrought to try the faith and prove the obedience of Israel. Signs come from a root meaning to come near, and he takes them for the tokens of God's continual presence, particularly the pillar of cloud and of fire that kept near them night and day and showed them when and where to pitch. Wonders he derives from a root meaning to persuade, and takes for persuasive facts and events, whether strictly miraculous or not, probably including typical representations. War he identifies with the engagements against the Amalekites, the Amorites and the Bashanites, in which the hand of God was seen rather than the hand of man. The mighty hand he describes as one strong to deal its blows, irresistible in its operations, grasping its enemies so that they cannot escape and protecting its friends so that they cannot be injured — for neither stratagem nor policy was used in this business, but the openly displayed power of God.

The stretched-out arm draws his most careful distinction, and it is a small vocabulary of scripture set in order. The finger of God denotes any manifestation of divine power beyond the reach of art or nature; the hand of God, the same power put forth in a more signal manner; the arm of God, omnipotence manifested in the most stupendous miracles; and the arm stretched out, that same omnipotence exerted in a continuation of such miracles, both in judgment and in mercy — which is the sense he takes here, the judgments poured out on Egypt and the mercies wrought for Israel being one continuous action. The last term, great terrors, he refers to the dismay produced by the ten plagues, noting that the Greek translators rendered it instead as great or portentous sights. Wesley organises the same list differently, taking temptations as the general title which the following particulars explain, and calling them trials because they tested both Egyptians and Israelites, whether they would be induced to believe and obey God or not; the terrors he takes as raised in the minds of the Egyptians by the terrible things done among them.
35:
Two verses give the purpose of everything just recited, and it is knowledge. Gill keeps the reference concrete — what was shown was what the Lord did in Egypt. Calvin draws out the argument in two steps. God had so proved his divinity by miracles and prodigies that the Israelites might know certainly that he was God; and from that Calvin concludes the second clause, that he is the only God. His reasoning is that although God's holy name is torn in pieces by various opinions, while each man manufactures his own gods for himself, it remains sure that the power and dominion of God cannot be withdrawn from him but reside in a single subject — so that the essence of the one God overthrows and annihilates all the other deities we foolishly invent. This, he says, must be carefully remarked, for it has been the common error of every age to seek a mixture of many gods, whereas all such imaginations should vanish before the brightness of the true God.

The second verse raises a small difficulty which Calvin takes seriously. The voice is said to have come out of heaven, and also out of the midst of the fire on the mountain; how do the two accord? His answer is that Moses simply means that the voice which flowed out of the fire into the people's ears was distinguished by plain indications which proved it to be heavenly. The fire was where they heard it; heaven was where it came from.

Gill weighs the same clause and offers two possibilities without settling between them. Thunder is the voice of God, by which he instructs men in the greatness of his power; or else what is meant is his voice in giving the law, which was for the instruction of Israel — though that voice, he notes, was heard on earth, on Mount Sinai, as the rest of the verse goes on to say.
