Keil and Delitzsch fix the geography plainly enough — the Lord had spoken to Israel chiefly down from heaven, and out of the great fire in which he had come down upon Sinai — and then dispute the verb that follows. Schultz took it to mean instructing the people with regard to God's truth and sovereignty. They prefer Knobel's rendering, that it means to take them under holy discipline: to inspire them with a salutary fear of the holiness of God's ways and of his judgments, by the awful phenomena which accompanied his descent and shadowed forth the sublime majesty of his nature. On that reading the teaching in this verse is not information conveyed but a fear instilled, and the fire is not a stage effect but part of the lesson.
37:
The reason for all of it is now given, and it is not a reason Israel could take any credit for. Gill is careful about which fathers are meant: not their immediate fathers, whose carcasses fell in the wilderness and who did not enter the land because of unbelief, but their more remote ancestors — Abraham, who is called the friend of God; Isaac, the son of promise in whom the seed was called; and Jacob, of whom it is particularly said that he was loved, when Esau was hated. Ellicott states the doctrinal shape of the answer and notes that it is the shape this book always gives it: the reasons for God's choice of Israel are frequently stated in Deuteronomy, and always in such a way as to enforce the sovereignty of God and to show the Israelites that their own merit was in no way the ground of that choice.

Calvin allows that the sentence can be construed two ways, since the connecting particle stands both at the beginning of the verse and before the following clause. The reasons given may be read with what precedes, so that the meaning is that so many miracles were wrought because God had chosen Abraham and his seed; or, as others take it, that this people was honoured with so many blessings because God loved their fathers. In the main, he judges, there is little discrepancy, for what Moses wants to show either way is that whatever good things God has conferred on this people are free gifts. He insists on the force of the word love here — it expresses the favour that springs of mere generosity, so as to exclude all worthiness in the person beloved. To the objection that God's election is eternal and cannot be dated from a man's lifetime, Calvin answers that the seed of Abraham was separated from all nations because God had gratuitously adopted their father; and he adds the circumstance that magnifies the blessing further, that God preferred this ignoble people to great and mighty nations whose own worthiness could not have acquired his favour.

Keil and Delitzsch take up the same construction question and reject two solutions before offering their own. The clause is not dependent on what precedes, as Schultz supposes; nor are these two verses the protasis with what follows as the apodosis, as Knobel maintains — both forms of construction, they say, are forced and unnatural. The verses form an independent thought, and the most important point of the whole address, the one that was to bind Israel to faithfulness toward Jehovah, is set out here as its sum and substance. On their reading the chain runs unbroken from the love of God for three men to the possession of a country: because he loved the fathers he chose their seed, and brought Israel out of Egypt by his own presence with great power, to drive out nations and to bring them in and give them the land — so that they might know it, take it to heart, and keep his laws.

Gill identifies the nations to be driven out as the seven of Canaan, greater in number and mightier in power than Israel; and he notes that the process had already begun, since the Amorites under Sihon and Og were dispossessed and their kingdoms already in Israel's hands. The argument of the passage therefore stands on ground the hearers were camped on.
39:
The sermon ends with a command to know something and a command to do something. Gill separates the two verbs in the first: own and acknowledge it now with the mouth, and lay it up and consider it in the heart hereafter, as a truth of the greatest importance, to be professed and held fast, thought upon continually and never forgotten. Ellicott sharpens the second verb by its use elsewhere — "consider" is the word rendered impute and account in Paul's argument to the Romans, so that Israel is being told to reckon with the fact rather than merely admit it. The thing to be reckoned with is that Jehovah is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath, and that there is none else.

Ellicott makes that a live argument rather than a formula. Do not indulge any polytheistic notions about the Deity: if every nation has its separate deity, how is it that Jehovah controls them all? His various dealings with Egyptians, Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites and Amorites, as well as with Israelites and Canaanites, mark him as Lord of all. And he presses the negative clause into an argument of its own — there are no more gods, so that if you desire to leave him behind, there is no one else to serve.

Henry draws out both halves of the geography. Jehovah is God in heaven above, Lord of all the hosts of the upper world; and God on the earth beneath, which, though distant from the throne of his glory, is not out of reach of his sight or his power, and though mean is not beneath his care. All the deities of the heathen, Henry observes, were counterfeits and usurpers, and not one of them so much as pretended to be a universal monarch in heaven and earth; they were only local. He also explains why Moses commands consideration and not merely knowledge: there are many things we know but are not the better for, because we do not consider them or draw the proper inferences. This one is a truth so evident that it cannot but be known, and so influential that, duly considered, it would effectually reform the world.

Calvin follows the same order and makes the second verse the point of the first. Moses desires them to consider carefully what God had shown them, because in so plain a matter there could be no excuse for error or ignorance; and he then reminds them why God would be known — that they might keep his law and obey his statutes. The sum, Calvin says, is that they would be inexcusable if they did not obediently receive a law they knew to have come from God, since they must be worse than stupid if a majesty attested by so many proofs did not awaken them to reverence. And lest they should undervalue the doctrine as coming from a mortal man, Moses expressly confesses that he is only the minister, and that he had set nothing before them which he had not received from God.

Gill grounds the obedience partly in obligation for all the good things done for them, and chiefly in the fact that the LORD is God in heaven and earth and so has a right to command; Keil and Delitzsch attach the promise, that it might go well with them and their children and their days be long in the land. Henry observes that this is the argument Moses began with and the one he closes on, and draws the conclusion that their prosperity would depend on their piety.
41:
The sermon is over, and what follows is an administrative act. Gill dates it: Moses severed the three cities when he had conquered the two Amorite kingdoms which God had given for an inheritance to Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh. He records a rabbinic qualification too — Jarchi and other Jewish writers held that no one was actually received into these three until the corresponding three in Canaan had been set apart for the same use, so that the refuge system did not begin to operate until it was complete. Henry names the three by their tribes, one in the lot of Reuben, one in Gad, one in the half tribe of Manasseh; Gill notes that Bezer in the wilderness is described elsewhere as on the plain, and takes it to be in the plains of Moab.

Calvin explains the principle he sees at work, and it is the most practical lesson anyone draws from the passage. God had appointed six cities of refuge in all, for anyone who had killed a man and could prove his innocence before the judges. As to the three on this side of Jordan, Moses records that he faithfully performed what God commanded. From which it appears that although he could not immediately comply with the command to its full extent, he did not wait until the other three could be added, but discharged his duty as far as circumstances permitted. Let us learn from this, Calvin says, that even when we cannot at once entirely carry out what God commands, we are by no means to be idle; for nothing but sheer laziness stands in our way, unless we promptly begin at God's command what it is his will to finish by the hands of others.

Henry finds the same lesson in the man rather than the institution: what Moses could do for that people while he was still with them, he did — and he did it partly to give an example to the rulers who would be settled in office after him, that they might observe such duties the better when he was gone. Keil and Delitzsch ask instead why the notice is inserted here at all, between the first address and the second, and answer it in three ways. Moses set the cities apart at this time because God had commanded it; doing so gave the land on that side its full consecration and thoroughly confirmed the possession of the two Amorite kingdoms; and in this punctual observance of a duty devolving on him he gave the people an example for their own conscientious observance of the Lord's commandments.

Gill notes the limit built into the provision — the slayer might flee there, but not any slayer, only the one who killed his neighbour unawares and had not hated him in time past. Clarke, referring the substance of the law back to its original statement in Numbers 35:11, adds the reading that the names of these cities have been thought to express some attribute of the Redeemer, since the cities of refuge are generally understood as types of the salvation provided in Christ for sinners. He also records a conjecture the other witnesses do not share, that the last nine verses of the chapter were added by either Joshua or Ezra.
44:
A heading is placed here, and the first question is what it heads. Gill answers it flatly: this is not the law concerning the cities of refuge just mentioned, but the law of the ten commandments repeated in the following chapter — and he cites Jarchi to the same effect, that the reference is to what Moses was about to set in order after this section. Wesley says the same in fewer words, that this is more punctually expressed in the following chapter, to which these words are a preface. Keil and Delitzsch treat the two verses as a general notice followed by a fuller description of the law according to its leading features — testimonies, statutes and rights — together with a note of the place and time at which the address was delivered.

Henry describes the transition as a preacher would. What follows is another sermon, probably preached the next sabbath day, when the congregation attended to receive instruction; the previous chapter exhorted them to obedience in general, and now Moses comes to repeat the law they were to observe, for he demands a universal but not an implicit obedience. His question is the practical one — how can we do our duty if we do not know it? So he sets the law before them as the rule they were to work by and the way they were to walk in; and as the glass in which they were to see their natural face, that looking into this perfect law of liberty they might continue in it.

Gill dates the material twice over, and the two dates are the point. These laws, moral and ceremonial and judicial, were delivered to Moses at Mount Sinai in the third month after they came out of Egypt, and he declared them then; and now, near forty years afterwards, he repeats them in the plains of Moab. Keil and Delitzsch add a precise reading of the phrase about coming out of Egypt: it does not mean after they had come out, but during the march, before they had reached the goal of their journeyings — that is, while they were still on the far side of the Jordan.

Calvin explains why a second promulgation was needed at all, and finds the reason in the hearers' situation rather than in the text. The law was published anew when the people had reached the threshold of the promised land, so that they might be the more disposed to obedience; and this is why their dwelling-place is mentioned, since the taste of a favour already received ought to stir up zeal to go on more cheerly. Two tribes and a half had by the conquest of the Amorites already obtained a resting-place and a home, and the assured possession of it lay before the eyes of the rest. But Calvin is careful to say what the repetition is not. Though Moses might explain the law at fuller length, nothing had been added to the summary originally promulgated; he rather indicates that whatever he taught them during the forty years had no other object than that they might keep the law of God more faithfully and exactly.
46:
The address is fixed to a place, and the place is described with a surveyor's care. Gill puts them in the valley over against Beth-peor, where Israel stayed for some time; the land is Sihon's, and Og's beside it, the two Amorite kings east of Jordan whose territory Israel had seized and divided as an inheritance among two tribes and a half. The boundaries are then given: from Aroer, a city of Moab on the bank of the Arnon which formed the Moabite border, as far as Mount Sion, and all the plain on the east of Jordan to the sea of the plain — which Gill identifies as the salt sea, the sea of Sodom — under the springs of Pisgah, which Gill takes for the streams rising from Mount Pisgah, the place elsewhere called Ashdoth-pisgah.

Henry finds the two halves of the description saying something. The first names an idol-temple of the Moabites, which perhaps Moses sometimes looked toward as he spoke, with a particular caution to Israel against the infection of that and other such dangerous places. The second names their own new conquest, the very land they had taken out of the hands of Sihon and Og and were now actually in possession of. So the sermon against images was preached within sight of a shrine, on ground that had just been given them; and their present triumphs, Henry says, were a powerful argument for the obedience it demanded.
